Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2025-08-07 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Luis (Redwood SE), Priya (SignalCraft Head of ML), Tom (CTO), Aisha (Infra)

Summary:
High-level intake to understand SignalCraft's cost sensitivity for a conversational summarization product. Priya emphasized token-heavy workloads (long contexts, lots of generations) and a hard monthly burn cap. Team evaluated tradeoffs between Redwood Hosted for speed vs Dedicated for predictable burn and Private (VPC/HSM) for data residency. Agreed to run a short micro-benchmark pilot; Redwood to send detailed cost sheet and security docs.

Topics covered: per-token price, how batching/caching reduces bills, residency options, demo/pilot scope, audit & encryption requirements.

--- Transcript: (timestamps approximate, auto-generated)
[00:00] Maya: All right, hi everyone, thanks for making time — we, uh, really appreciate it. I'm Maya, I'm the AE on this account, and with me is Luis, our solutions engineer.
[00:05] Luis: Hey team, quick wave. I'll mostly be doing the deep-dive on the runtime and benchmarks.
[00:10] Priya: Hi hi, thanks. We have a fairly tight budget this year so trying to figure out where Redwood fits — is it going to blow our burn on tokens or actually save us money vs self-hosting.
[00:16] Tom: Yep, and we need to keep PII in our environment, so VPC or private deployment is likely.
[00:20] Aisha: Also curious about KMS key rotation and audit trails for compliance.
[00:25] Maya: Great — we'll run through per-token pricing, the levers you can use — batching, prefix/KV cache, quantization suggestions — and then how those change with Hosted, Dedicated, and Private.
[00:30] Priya: Quick context — our product creates multi-paragraph summaries from meeting transcripts, average prompt+completion is roughly 1,500 tokens, sometimes up to 4k; we expect 50k calls/month in Q4 if things go well.
[00:40] Luis: Okay that's helpful — 1.5k average is sizable. With Redwood Hosted our published per-token rate is X (note: rep recites rough hosted pricing), but the real lever is effective tokens per request after batching and cache.
[00:55] Priya: When you say cache, you mean the KV cache for autoregressive tokens? We have a lot of shared prefixes — like boilerplate context — will that help?
[01:02] Luis: Yes, exactly. Our KV/prefix cache stores repeated key/value states so that for similar contexts, the model reuses cached KV and avoids recomputing earlier tokens. In practice for summarization with recurring templates you can see 20-40% token delta reduction in some workloads.
[01:15] Tom: But that's more effective for streaming or synchronous flows? Our product is mostly synchronous API calls from the app.
[01:22] Luis: It's applicable — the cache works for both streaming and non-streaming requests. The trick is traffic shape: if you have many identical preambles then cache hit rate is high.
[01:30] Priya: What about batching? Our latency SLOs are 400 ms p95 — if you batch aggressively to save tokens cost, will you exceed that?
[01:39] Luis: There's a tradeoff. Continuous batching in Redwood collects for a short micro-window and can give 10-30% token savings without pushing p95 above the 200–500ms envelope on beefy GPUs. But at 400ms SLO you can only batch lightly. For lower SLOs you can batch more.
[01:53] Maya: So in summary, caching helps reduce compute per request, batching helps throughput and amortizes startup cost per token, and quantization reduces GPU cost if you self-host or run Dedicated.
[02:03] Aisha: For Dedicated — how predictable is the monthly bill? We get charged even if we underutilize?
[02:10] Maya: Dedicated is a reserved capacity model — you commit to a pool and that gives predictable monthly commitment. You can configure autoscaling and burst outside of the commit but that can add variable charges. So it's great if you can forecast steady throughput.
[02:22] Tom: Would Dedicated be hosted by Redwood in our cloud or on our infra?
[02:27] Luis: For Redwood Dedicated we run the capacity in our managed fleet but isolated for you. For Private we can ship a VPC-controlled deployment or on-prem package where compute sits in your account.
[02:36] Priya: Okay, so Private (VPC) looks necessary for data residency. How different are the unit economics between Private and Hosted?
[02:43] Luis: Private has additional infra ops cost and typically higher per-token compute cost since you're responsible for the underlying hardware or cloud markup; but you save on egress/data residency and you have full control over KMS/HSM. Hosted has the lowest unit price per token because of multi-tenant efficiency. Dedicated sits between: predictable monthly but higher than hosted per-token.
[03:00] Priya: Is there a ballpark % difference?
[03:03] Luis: Ballpark — hosted might be baseline X, dedicated might be ~1.3–1.6x hosted depending on commitment, and private ~1.5–2x hosted depending on your infra and support level. We'll put exact numbers in the spreadsheet.
[03:16] Tom: We need example math with our workload: 50k calls/month at 1.5k tokens average.
[03:23] Maya: Right — so that's about 75M tokens/month. If hosted per-token is 0.00008 (example) that gives a baseline; but with a conservative 25% caching/batching we can drop it significantly. We'll model a few scenarios in the sheet.
[03:38] Priya: Real question: our CFO says a hard cap of $X/month for model infra. If we choose hosted but go over budget, what's the safety/fallback?
[03:48] Maya: You can set hard quotas at the API level, route to cheaper variants on fallback, or route lower-priority traffic to a smaller model. We also support per-route budgets and emergency throttles.
[03:58] Aisha: About security: we need SOC2 Type II, SSO, SAML, RBAC for API keys in dev vs prod, and key material never leaving our KMS.
[04:08] Luis: We support SSO/SAML, RBAC, and for Private you can bring your KMS so keys never leave your environment. Hosted supports envelope encryption with customer-managed keys for many cases; we'll share our SOC2 cert and the network diagram.
[04:20] Priya: How do audit logs look? We need per-request traces and token-level cost breakdowns for billing back to product teams.
[04:27] Maya: Console includes per-route and per-token breakdowns, trace IDs, and you can export logs to your SIEM; we'll include a sample.
[04:35] Tom: For pilot scope — can we run maybe 10k calls, representative traffic, measure latency and effective tokens with and without caching?
[04:43] Luis: Yep, we usually do a micro-benchmark: you give sample payloads and a token distribution CSV, we run on hosted and dedicated (if needed) and send an analysis. Typically takes ~3–5 business days to run and compile.
[04:54] Priya: Any gotchas with quantization and generation quality? We care about quality — we can't lose summarization fidelity just to save tokens.
[05:02] Luis: Right. Quantization can slightly impact quality, but using Redwood's recommended profiles we saw negligible quality delta for many summarization models. We'll include eval prompts and metrics (ROUGE, human spot checks) in the pilot.
[05:14] Priya: If Dedicated is the option, how is rollback and model versioning handled? We want to test new checkpoints and revert if quality drops.
[05:22] Luis: Our rollout features support pinned versions, canary deployments, and automatic fallback to a previous variant if latency or quality regressions are detected. Works across Hosted/Dedicated/Private with the same APIs.
[05:33] Aisha: For VPC connection what about egress and private peering — do you support AWS PrivateLink or equivalent?
[05:40] Maya: Yes, for Private deployments we integrate with VPC peering or PrivateLink equivalents. We'll provide a network checklist for your infra team.
[05:47] Tom: Are there long-term savings if we move from Hosted to Dedicated once volume grows?
[05:52] Luis: Typically yes — once utilization crosses commit thresholds, Dedicated amortizes base costs better. We'll model at what token-per-month levels Dedicated becomes cheaper under your assumptions.
[06:02] Priya: Our acceptance criteria for vendor selection: within budget cap for Q4, p95 latency <= 400ms for cold path, ability to keep PII in-scope, and clear pilot metrics.
[06:12] Maya: Noted — we'll map those criteria in the follow-up.
[06:16] Priya: Any mention of competitor differences? We've seen OpenAI fine for prototyping but costs scale. Replicate seems cheaper for GPU spot usage but lacks enterprise features.
[06:26] Luis: Yup, we'll call out where Redwood's observability and routing give you guardrails that managed GPU vendors may not.
[06:31] (cross talk)
[06:35] Aisha: One last question — tokenization differences across models: do you normalize tokens for cost estimation?
[06:41] Luis: We normalize to model family tokenization in the spreadsheet; we also ask you to provide typical payloads so we can run real tokenization.
[06:47] Maya: Cool — do we have alignment on next steps and timeline?
[06:50] Tom: Yep, send the sheet and security docs, we'll provide sample traffic and decide on pilot dates.
[06:56] Maya: Great thanks everyone. We'll follow-up by Monday with the cost scenarios.
